vignette:
She is fifty-six, a married woman from Oceania, and she has spent most of her adult life in social ministry work, moving quietly toward people in crisis when others step back. In her church community, she is known as steady, prayerful, and practical. She visits families after funerals, sits with women when they have nowhere else to go, organizes food parcels, and answers late-night calls without sounding burdened. From the outside, her life still looks much the same. It is only over time, in the privacy of these sessions, that the shape of what she carries becomes clear.

The change begins one evening about three years ago, after a community outreach event. She stays late to clean up, stacking chairs and putting away donated clothing. A man she knows through ministry offers to help lock up. She remembers feeling mildly uneasy but brushing it aside; in her work she is used to overriding discomfort in order to be polite, to keep peace, to assume goodwill. Inside the storage room, his manner shifts. For a few stunned seconds she cannot make sense of what is happening. Then she understands and her body seems to stop belonging to her. She says no, tells him to stop, but her voice sounds far away. She later remembers the smell of dust, the scrape of a chair leg, the fluorescent light humming overhead. More than anything she remembers freezing—hating that she freezes, hating that she cannot force herself into the kind of resistance she imagines she should have shown.

Afterward she drives home in silence, gripping the steering wheel so hard her hands ache. When her husband asks why she is late, she says there was extra cleaning. That night she showers for a long time, scrubbing at her skin until it stings. She does not sleep. Each time she starts to drift off, she is back in the room, pinned by the same disbelief. By morning she has already begun telling herself a story she will repeat for months: that she misread things, that perhaps she was careless, that speaking about it would damage the ministry and shame her family.

In the weeks that follow, she throws herself harder into work. She answers more calls, volunteers for extra visits, fills her calendar so completely that there is almost no unstructured time. But her body does not cooperate with the plan to move on. She startles when a man steps too close behind her. If she hears a door click shut, her chest tightens instantly. She begins checking rooms when she enters them, noticing exits, making sure she is never the last person left behind. In meetings she finds herself drifting, then suddenly flooded by an image so vivid she loses track of what is being said. Sometimes she feels as though she is watching herself from a distance, nodding and offering comfort while something frightened and wordless hides underneath.

At home, her husband notices she has changed before he knows why. She used to be affectionate, quick to lean against him in the kitchen or reach for his hand in bed. Now she stiffens at unexpected touch. She starts sleeping near the edge of the mattress and tells him she is just tired, just stressed. He asks if she is angry with him. She says no, then feels guilty for withholding the truth. The guilt grows into a private loneliness. She sits at church hearing sermons about trust and forgiveness and feels suddenly cut off from the language that once grounded her. She still prays, but often the prayers feel mechanical, as if spoken from very far away.

Over time her world narrows in careful, almost invisible ways. She avoids being alone with male colleagues. She changes her route through the ministry building so she does not pass the storage room. If she has to unlock a room by herself, her heart races and her fingers fumble at the keys. Some nights she wakes drenched in sweat after dreams that are not exact replays, but carry the same terror and helplessness. On those nights she walks through the house checking windows and doors, then sits in the dark at the kitchen table until dawn, listening for sounds that do not come.

What troubles her nearly as much as the memories is the shift in how she sees herself. She has built a life around being a refuge for others, yet now she feels fragile, watchful, and ashamed. When women in ministry confide experiences of violence, she can offer them compassion that she cannot extend to herself. She thinks she should be stronger by now. Instead she finds herself snapping at small things, forgetting appointments, feeling exhausted by the ordinary demands of the day. There are moments during pastoral visits when a familiar cologne, a certain laugh, or even the scrape of a chair across a floor sends her mind and body back without warning.

She eventually tells her husband in fragments, stopping and starting, eyes fixed on her hands. He weeps, then grows quiet with anger on her behalf. His tenderness helps, but it also makes the reality harder to keep contained. Now, in the present, she continues her ministry work, still showing up for others, still carrying meals, making calls, offering prayer. But she does so with a constant undercurrent of vigilance. She wants her life back—the ease in her body, the trust in her own instincts, the sense that the world is not always about to close in. Even in safe rooms, part of her remains braced, listening, waiting, and trying to understand how one night continues to live inside her.
